text.p: Faint hopes of an imminent cut in German interest rates were dashed on Wednesday as two leading members of the Bundesbank's council poured cold water on prospects for a move lower.

In an unusually categorical statement on monetary policy, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said there was no reason to expect further cuts in key German interest rates, prompting rapid declines in stock and bond prices.
"Key rates are at a historic low and here nothing more is to be expected or necessary," Issing, the central bank's chief economist, said in an interview on German television.

Later, Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum reinforced the message as he told reporters in the early evening that current economic conditions and M3 money supply data indicated that present interest rate levels were correct.

After a rapid decline as Issing's remarks hit the screens, the December future on 10-year German bonds closed down about a third of a point at 99.47 while the IBIS DAX index ended down 42.85 points, or 1.57 percent, at 2,678.89.
The comments had particular impact as they came directly ahead of Thursday's twice-monthly meeting of the German central bank's council.
"It was a more explicit view and the market obviously saw it that way," said Armin Kayser, an economist at Swiss Bank Corp in Frankfurt.

"Issing was taking into account the fact that the economy was buoyant in the third quarter," said Uwe Angenendt, an economist at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt. "There is no need for further interest rate cuts."
Issing told Germany's ZDF channel that the German economy was performing better than expected at the start of 1996 and there was reason to believe that the upswing would continue into next year.
Economists said the remarks seemed aimed at preventing bond prices from becoming further inflated by unjustified expectations of more rate cuts.

"Issing's comments are positive in that they should counter false bond market expectations," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt. "It should let some air out of the bond price bubble."
Economists predicted that key interest rates would remain unchanged until well into 1997 because there was virtually no danger of an early upturn in inflation, now around 1.5 percent.
Besides, the easing of the mark against the dollar in recent weeks had made life easier for German exporters, thereby stimulating the economy in the same way a rate cut would.
The Bundesbank last trimmed its main money market rate, or repo, by 30 basis points to a historic low of three percent at the end of August.
Its discount and Lombard rates, seen as setting the floor and ceiling to German money market rates, have been at 2.50 percent and 4.50 percent respectively since April.
Gaddum said the Bundesbank's goal was to hold rates steady for as long as possible, pending fresh economic data.
Recent comments by other Bundesbank officials have also dampened prospects for further interest rate cuts but have been less categorical.
Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said earlier this month he did not see a need for another cut in German interest rates but added "you never can tell. Never say never."
